data.name: Stage_Journey_Nav
data.value: The stages of the testing journey

data.name: Stage_Planning_Lead
data.value: Decide what will be tested, how thoroughly, and what has to be true before anybody calls it done.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Why
data.value: Most teams do plan, in a document nobody opens again. The plan matters because it is the only place the words “enough testing” are ever given a meaning — and if that meaning is not written down before the work starts, it gets decided at the end, under pressure, by whoever is most tired.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point1_Text
data.value: What is in, what is deliberately out, and how each part will be tested. The “deliberately out” half is the one that saves an argument later.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point2_Text
data.value: What could go wrong, how likely it is and what it would cost. Testing effort follows that rating rather than following habit.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point3_Text
data.value: The conditions for starting and for stopping, agreed in advance and checked against reality at the end.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Today
data.value: Not built. Planning lives in the roadmap, not in the product: there is no plan editor, no risk register and no criteria to check against. The pages above describe what is intended, not what you can use.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Lead
data.value: Turn requirements into things that can actually be checked, and keep the thread from each requirement to the tests that cover it.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Why
data.value: A requirement that cannot be checked is not a requirement, it is a hope. Reading requirements for testability is the cheapest defect-finding there is: it costs an afternoon and it finds the contradictions before anybody has written code against them.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point1_Text
data.value: Each requirement read for the things that make it untestable: a missing number, an undefined “fast”, two sentences that cannot both be true.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point2_Text
data.value: The distinct things worth checking about a requirement, named before anybody writes a step. This is where coverage is decided.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point3_Title
data.value: A traceability matrix that is not a spreadsheet

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point3_Text
data.value: Requirements against tests, with the gaps visible, kept current because it is derived rather than maintained by hand.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Today
data.value: Not built. There is no requirement, no test condition and no matrix in the product yet. The data model for them is designed and written down; none of it is running.

data.name: Stage_Design_Lead
data.value: Work out the actual cases: which inputs, which boundaries, which combinations, and what data they need.

data.name: Stage_Design_Why
data.value: Test design is where testing stops being a feeling and becomes a technique. Boundary values, equivalence classes, decision tables and state transitions are not academic: they are the difference between forty tests that all check the same thing and twelve that check twelve different things.

data.name: Stage_Design_Point1_Text
data.value: Boundaries, equivalence classes, decision tables, state transitions — chosen for the problem rather than used out of habit.

data.name: Stage_Design_Point2_Text
data.value: Steps, expected results and the reason the case exists, versioned, so a change to a test is as reviewable as a change to code.

data.name: Stage_Design_Point3_Text
data.value: What each case needs to exist before it runs, described with the case instead of being improvised on the day.

data.name: Stage_Design_Today
data.value: Not built. No test case library and no AI-assisted design exist in the product. A planner that turns a scenario in plain words into executable steps does exist and is measured — see the capability page — but it is not case design.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Lead
data.value: Run the tests against a real application in a real browser, and keep enough evidence that a failure can be acted on without being reproduced first.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Why
data.value: A run that says “failed” and nothing else sends a person back to reproduce it, which is where most of the cost of a defect is. A run worth having names the step, keeps the screenshot of the moment it went wrong, and distinguishes the application being broken from the test infrastructure being broken.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point1_Title
data.value: Every ending has its own name

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point1_Text
data.value: Passed, failed, stopped, out of time, over budget, could not run. A run that hit its budget is not a failing application, and calling it one would make the failure rate a lie.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point2_Text
data.value: A screenshot and a timestamp for each step, so the failure arrives with the picture of what the application actually showed.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point3_Title
data.value: The browser runs where it cannot reach anything

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point3_Text
data.value: Out of process, behind a proxy that refuses every address but the one being tested, judging where a connection actually goes rather than what it is called.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Today
data.value: Built, and the only stage that is. A browser is driven against a real application out of process, runs are stored with their steps and screenshots, and one organization cannot see another’s. What is not built: a container for each run, and any target other than our own demo application.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Lead
data.value: Report what went wrong so that somebody can fix it, and keep the link back to the test and the requirement it came from.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Why
data.value: Most of the time lost to a defect is spent on the round trip: a report too thin to act on, a developer who cannot reproduce it, a tester who has moved on. A defect raised out of a run already carries the steps, the evidence and the environment, which removes the round trip rather than speeding it up.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point1_Text
data.value: The failing step, its screenshot and its timings become the report, so nothing has to be described twice or from memory.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point2_Text
data.value: Triage, severity and status that mean the same thing to everyone, with the history of who changed what kept.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point3_Text
data.value: From the defect to the test, the requirement and the run; and from a requirement to every defect found against it.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Today
data.value: Not built. A failed run keeps its step, message and screenshot, which is the raw material; there is no defect record, no triage and no synchronisation with an issue tracker.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Lead
data.value: Say what the testing found, what it did not cover, and whether the exit criteria agreed at the start have actually been met.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Why
data.value: The question at the end is always the same: do we ship? A report answers it badly by counting tests, and well by comparing what was found against what was agreed — including the parts nobody tested, which is the number most reports quietly leave out.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point1_Text
data.value: What was tested against what was planned, with the untested parts named rather than omitted.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point2_Text
data.value: How results, flake and defect ages move over releases, because one run tells you almost nothing.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point3_Title
data.value: A readiness decision with its reasons attached

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point3_Text
data.value: The exit criteria, which of them hold, and who signed it off — kept, so the decision can be reviewed afterwards.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Today
data.value: Not built. Runs are stored, so the data a report would draw on is beginning to exist; there are no dashboards, no trends and no readiness report.
